Floyd David Moore, chief of the IRS Intelligence Division's New Orleans district, swore an affidavit about a meeting held on May 29, 1969. His visitor was Pershing Gervais, the former Garrison investigator. The subject of their talk was payoffs to Louisiana public officials.

An affidavit from a tax intelligence chief is a serious paper: sworn, specific, and filed for use. Gervais moved between the district attorney's office and the underworld it investigated, and a meeting about payoffs put him on the federal record. Moore's statement preserves that meeting as the IRS chief swore it happened.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, died in 2022, and the Archive published this memorial. Its opening line is unsparing about his country after him. Gorbachev ended the Cold War, only to see party apparatchiks destroy his country, a process the posting says continues.

The memorial's second claim fits the Archive's mission: Gorbachev made history, then freed history by opening his documents. Few leaders have given archivists more. His papers and his foundation's records underpin many of the Archive's Russia publications. An institution built on documents marking his death in those terms is both tribute and a fair statement of his documentary legacy.

Before NATO enlarged eastward, Western leaders spoke with Mikhail Gorbachev about the alliance's future as Germany reunified. What he was told, and whether it amounted to a promise, became a lasting dispute. This briefing-book page presents the record of what Gorbachev heard. Its companion volume covers what Boris Yeltsin heard later in the decade. The evidence here is the title alone. Read together, the two volumes let readers compare the assurances themselves rather than the claims made about them.

Anatoly Chernyaev, the Soviet aide whose diaries became one of the great insider sources on the Cold War's end, was born in 1921. The National Security Archive marked his centennial, the hundredth anniversary of his birth, with a briefing book page honoring the man and the record he left behind. Chernyaev served Mikhail Gorbachev and wrote down what he saw. Only the page capture survives in this entry's evidence, but its subject is the diarist, celebrated by the institution that has spent years publishing his work in English.

Noonan and Porter's report maps the risks and challenges across the full deployment cycle, from send-off to return. It pairs each challenge with evidence-based strategies that actually help veterans land on their feet.

20505-what-s-in-the-new-york-evening-jou:
What's in the New York Evening Journal?, published in 1928, is a promotional book about William Randolph Hearst's great evening paper. It calls the Journal America's greatest evening newspaper. The book walks readers through its news, features, and comics.

Its star attraction was Arthur Brisbane, who wrote editorials for the paper for many years. His daily editorials, the book boasts, were one of the outstanding reasons nearly half of all New York newspaper buyers chose the Evening Journal. The volume is a period piece of press ballyhoo, showing how mass papers sold themselves.
